newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Saab Auto says to post loss in '96 - newsletter.
newsitem.headline: Saab Auto says to post loss in '96 - newsletter.

text.p: Swedish-U.S. car maker Saab Automobile AB posted a loss in 1996, a company newsletter quoted Saab Automobile managing director Robert Hendry as saying.
"1996 ended with a loss. Our long-term goal is a profit equal to six percent of sales," Saab Nu quoted Hendry as saying.
Saab Automobile is due to publish its results around 1100 GMT on Friday.
Development of Saab Automobile's dealer network is an important challenge for Saab in 1997, especially considering the company is due to debut its new model this year, the newsletter said.
"The launch of our new model is the most critical challenge in 1997," Hendry told Saab Nu.

The car maker, which is jointly owned by U.S. automotive group General Motors and Swedish investment group Investor AB, posted a loss of 1.24 billion crowns ($168.2 million) after tax but before extraordinary items, compared with a break even result in 1995.

Turnover fell in 1996 by 1.4 percent to 19.68 billion crowns and the operating result swung to a loss of 658 million crowns from a profit of 737 million crowns. This corresponds to an operating margin of -3.3 percent, compared to 3.7 percent.

This 1996 result reflected a loss of 749 million crowns before tax and extraordinary items for the second half of the year compared to a loss of 47 million crowns a year earlier and a rise in turnover by six percent to 9.55 billion crowns.

"As a step towards financial reconstruction the 1996 result improved by 999 million crowns through an extraordinary item mainly through the write-down of certain debts to shareholders," Saab Automobile said in a statement.
Saab's owners agreed in June to each invest 1.74 billion crowns in Saab Auto in 1996-97 in a bid to boost sales by 50 percent over five years and reverse the poor performance of recent years.
Hendry said in the results statement that the decrease in 1996 from a year earlier depended on factors including higher costs for product development.

"These were considerably higher marketing costs to increase consciousness about Saab as an exclusive car mark, strengthening our dealership network on important markets as well as unfavourable effects of the stronger crown which reduced our profit margins on export markets, and higher costs for product development," Hendry said.
Sales fell 0.7 percent to 98,000 cars in 1996, the company said.

"Decreases in Sweden, Italy and the Asia-Pacific region were counterbalanced by sales increases on several important markets such as the U.S. (an increase of 11 percent), Britain (+29 percent) and France (+30 percent)."
Saab Automobile said the U.S. was its largest market and sales there totalled 28,300 cars, followed by Sweden with 15,600 cars, Britain with 14,900 and Italy with 5,000.
Uncertainty about a change in rules regarding company cars was behind a decrease in Swedish sales.
"Sales in Sweden -- which are based heavily on sales of company cars -- decreased by 15 percent because of uncertainty during the year on tax rules for private use of such cars," Saab said.
"New rules were set at the end of the year and demand on new cars is expected to increase in Sweden in 1997," it said.
It said sales of its 900 model rose four percent to 64,300, of which 14,200 were the Saab 900 Cabriolet. Sales of the 9000 model fell 10 percent to 33,700 cars.
($ = 7.373 Swedish Crowns) -- Abigail Schmelz, Stockholm newsroom +46-8-700-1003
